questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department minutes after eating shrimp at a restaurant. He has diffuse hives, swelling of the eyelids, and difficulty breathing with audible wheezing. His blood pressure is low. Which of the following mechanisms is most directly responsible for his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell killing of epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes in small vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG antibody blocking a cell-surface receptor

explanation.summary: Rapid-onset anaphylaxis after a food trigger is a type 1 (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction driven by IgE cross-linking on mast cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a sensitized person, allergen cross-links IgE bound to the high-affinity FcεRI receptor on mast cells, triggering degranulation. Preformed mediators such as histamine and leukotrienes produce vasodilation, vascular leak, bronchoconstriction, and hives within minutes, which is the clinical picture of anaphylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T-cell killing is a type 4 delayed reaction that develops over 24-72 hours, far too slow for this acute presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement-mediated lysis of cells is a type 2 cytotoxic mechanism, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not the cause of an immediate allergic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 reaction that produces vasculitis, nephritis, or serum sickness over hours to days, not immediate anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An antibody blocking a receptor is the type 2 cellular dysregulation mechanism of myasthenia gravis, unrelated to acute food-triggered anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fatigue, joint pain, and a malar (facial) rash. Laboratory studies reveal antibodies directed against nuclear antigens and DNA, and she is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. A kidney biopsy shows granular glomerular deposits of IgG and complement. This disorder is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity reaction?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2, antibody against a cell-bound antigen

explanation.summary: SLE is a prototypical type 3 hypersensitivity in which autoantibodies against soluble self-antigens form immune complexes that deposit in tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SLE, autoantibodies recognize the host's own nuclei and DNA as foreign. These bind soluble self-antigens to form immune complexes that deposit in the skin, kidney glomeruli, joints, and bone marrow, driving complement activation and inflammation. Glomerular immune-complex deposits confirm a type 3 mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 reactions are IgE-mediated immediate allergic reactions, not driven by immune complexes against self-DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Molecular mimicry describes acute rheumatic fever (a type 2 reaction), not the immune-complex disease of lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type 2 reactions target antigens fixed to a specific cell or matrix, causing organ-specific damage, whereas lupus complexes are soluble and deposit at multiple sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 4 reactions are mediated by T cells over 24-72 hours, not by circulating antibody-antigen complexes.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman reports two weeks of drooping eyelids, double vision, and muscle weakness that worsens as the day goes on. She is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies continuously stimulate a cell-surface receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in muscle capillaries

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis is a type 2 hypersensitivity in which antibodies inhibit the acetylcholine receptor, a form of cellular dysregulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies specifically target acetylcholine receptors on the muscle cell surface. By blocking these receptors, they impair neuromuscular transmission and produce the characteristic fatigable weakness, without destroying the cell itself.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuous receptor stimulation describes Graves disease, in which antibodies activate the TSH receptor, the opposite of the inhibitory antibodies in myasthenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement-mediated cell destruction is a cytotoxic type 2 mechanism; myasthenia results from receptor blockade, not myocyte lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine release from mast cells is a type 1 allergic mechanism, unrelated to autoantibody-mediated muscle weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism and does not explain the receptor-specific weakness of myasthenia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old medical intern who recently cared for a patient with active tuberculosis has a tuberculin skin test (PPD) placed. Forty-eight to seventy-two hours later, a firm, raised, indurated area develops at the injection site. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune complex deposition with complement activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Memory T cells activating macrophages via IFN-gamma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preformed antibodies opsonizing the injected antigen

explanation.summary: The positive PPD is a type 4 (delayed) hypersensitivity mediated by memory T cells and macrophages, peaking at 48-72 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: The injected purified protein derivative is presented by dendritic cells and macrophages to memory CD4+ Th1 cells generated by prior TB exposure. These T cells secrete IFN-gamma (and provide CD40L) to activate macrophages, producing the local inflammation and induration seen at 48-72 hours, the delayed timing characteristic of a type 4 reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE cross-linking causes an immediate type 1 reaction within minutes, not a delayed indurated lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism producing vasculitis or serum sickness, not the induration of a PPD test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK-mediated ADCC is a type 2 cytotoxic mechanism and does not explain the T-cell-driven delayed skin reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opsonization by antibody is a type 2 mechanism; the PPD response is cell-mediated, not antibody-dependent.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid. She is found to have autoantibodies that bind the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. Which of the following best describes how these antibodies cause her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block the TSH receptor, reducing hormone output

choices.label: B
choices.text: They continuously activate the TSH receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: They fix complement and destroy thyroid follicular cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They form circulating immune complexes that deposit in the thyroid

choices.label: E
choices.text: They recruit cytotoxic T cells to kill thyrocytes

explanation.summary: Graves disease is a type 2 hypersensitivity in which antibodies continuously activate the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Graves disease, antibodies bind and persistently stimulate the TSH receptor on the thyroid gland. This continuous activation causes overproduction of thyroid hormones and hyperthyroidism, an example of antibody-mediated cellular dysregulation that amplifies rather than destroys cell function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor blockade producing reduced output describes an inhibitory antibody, as in myasthenia gravis, and would cause hypothyroid symptoms, not the hyperthyroidism seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement-mediated destruction of cells is a cytotoxic mechanism; Graves antibodies stimulate rather than lyse thyrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism and does not explain receptor-specific overstimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytotoxic T-cell killing is a type 4 mechanism and is not the basis of this antibody-driven overstimulation.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy develops migratory joint pain, a rash, and signs of cardiac inflammation three weeks after an untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. Which of the following best explains the cardiac involvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T-cell recognition of viral antigens displayed on myocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the myocardium and cardiac valves

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation within the cardiac tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complexes of streptococcal antigen depositing in the coronary vessel walls

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is a type 2 hypersensitivity caused by molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The group A streptococcal virulence factor M protein shares structural similarity with a human cardiac protein. Patients break tolerance and generate antibodies that bind both antigens; binding to cardiac cells produces the carditis of acute rheumatic fever, which appears a few weeks after the untreated infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This is a bacterial, not viral, trigger, and the damage is antibody-mediated rather than driven by cytotoxic T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute rheumatic fever is an immune-mediated reaction from molecular mimicry, not direct microbial invasion of the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE-driven mast cell degranulation is a type 1 allergic mechanism, unrelated to post-streptococcal carditis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism; rheumatic carditis results from cross-reactive antibodies binding cardiac tissue directly, not from deposited complexes.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has fatigue and jaundice. Laboratory studies show anemia, and a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for IgG on her erythrocytes. Her red cells are being removed primarily by splenic phagocytes rather than by intravascular complement lysis. Which of the following best explains why membrane attack complex formation is limited on her erythrocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocytes lack surface antigens for antibody binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG is unable to activate the complement cascade

choices.label: C
choices.text: NK cells consume complement during ADCC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regulatory proteins such as CD55 and CD59 inhibit MAC formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen removes all complement proteins from the circulation

explanation.summary: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia, complement regulators on red cells limit MAC formation, so opsonization and splenic phagocytosis dominate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies against erythrocyte blood-group antigens opsonize the cells, and FcR-expressing phagocytes in the spleen internalize and destroy them. The membrane attack complex is not a prominent mechanism because regulatory proteins such as CD55 and CD59 block substantial MAC formation on the erythrocyte surface.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes do carry surface (blood-group) antigens, which is exactly what the autoantibodies target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG can activate complement and act as an opsonin; the issue is regulation of MAC on the cell surface, not an inability to trigger complement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK cells mediate ADCC using perforin and granzymes and do not consume complement to limit MAC formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen removes opsonized cells by phagocytosis; it does not strip complement proteins from the blood.

questions.stem: A patient is treated with a large dose of horse-derived antivenom after a snakebite. Ten days later she develops fever, joint pain, a rash, and cutaneous vasculitis. Serum studies show decreased C3 and C4. Which of the following best describes the underlying process?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies against the patient's own receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct complement-mediated lysis of the patient's leukocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation and tissue deposition of immune complexes

explanation.summary: Serum sickness is the prototypical type 3 reaction, in which antibodies against foreign proteins form immune complexes that deposit and consume complement.
explanation.whyCorrect: About one to two weeks after exposure to a large amount of foreign protein (here, horse serum antivenom), the patient's immune system makes antibodies that form immune complexes. These deposit in vessels, skin, and joints and activate complement widely, which is why serum C3 and C4 fall. Snakebite antitoxin is a classic modern trigger of serum sickness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A delayed contact reaction is a type 4 cell-mediated response (e.g., poison ivy), not the immune-complex, complement-consuming picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoantibodies against self-receptors describe a type 2 cellular dysregulation disorder, not a reaction to injected foreign protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct complement lysis of the patient's own leukocytes is a cytotoxic type 2 mechanism and does not explain the systemic immune-complex syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis occurs within minutes of exposure, not 10 days later, and would not lower C3 and C4.

questions.stem: Two days after hiking, a 22-year-old man develops an intensely itchy, linear rash with small blisters on his forearms where plant leaves brushed his skin. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A small molecule acts as a hapten and primes memory T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE bound to mast cells cross-links and releases histamine within minutes

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG antibodies opsonize skin cells for phagocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complexes deposit in dermal blood vessels within hours

explanation.summary: Poison ivy contact dermatitis is a type 4 delayed hypersensitivity triggered by a hapten that primes T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poison ivy leaves contain pentadecylcatechol, a small lipid-soluble molecule that penetrates the skin and acts as a hapten by binding skin proteins. This primes T cells and generates memory; on subsequent exposure, memory T cells are activated to produce contact dermatitis, with vesicles and blistering appearing over 24-72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoantibodies activating cell-surface receptors describe type 2 cellular dysregulation (e.g., Graves disease), not contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causes immediate reactions within minutes, not a blistering rash appearing two days later.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization for phagocytosis is a type 2 antibody mechanism, not the cause of contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism producing vasculitis, not a hapten-driven delayed skin reaction.

questions.stem: A patient collapses with hypotension and bronchospasm shortly after a bee sting. To help confirm that mast cell degranulation occurred, measurement of which of the following is most useful?

explanation.summary: Tryptase is released only by mast cells, making it a useful clinical marker of mast cell degranulation in suspected anaphylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tryptase is a protease stored in mast cell granules and released during degranulation. Because it comes specifically from mast cells, its serum level is clinically helpful in evaluating patients with suspected anaphylaxis and mast cell disorders, such as this patient with a bee-sting reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-nuclear antibodies are markers of systemic lupus erythematosus, a type 3 immune-complex disease, not mast cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD16 on NK cells mediates antibody-dependent cytotoxicity in type 2 reactions and is not a marker of mast cell degranulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatoid factor is an autoantibody associated with rheumatoid arthritis, unrelated to anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low C3 and C4 indicate complement consumption in immune-complex (type 3) disease, not mast cell degranulation.

questions.stem: In one mechanism of type 2 hypersensitivity, IgG bound to a cell-surface antigen is recognized by CD16 (Fc-gamma-RIII) on natural killer cells, which then release perforin and granzymes to kill the target cell. This process is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Membrane attack complex formation on the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opsonization and phagocytosis of the cell

explanation.summary: NK-cell killing of antibody-coated target cells via CD16 is antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).
explanation.whyCorrect: In ADCC, IgG bound to a cell-surface antigen is detected by CD16 (Fc-gamma-RIII) on natural killer cells. This binding activates the NK cell to release perforin and granzymes, which induce apoptosis in the target cell. It is one of the cytotoxic effector mechanisms of type 2 hypersensitivity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Delayed-type hypersensitivity is a type 4 T-cell-mediated reaction, not an antibody-directed NK response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism involving soluble antigen, not antibody-coated target cells killed by NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membrane attack complex is a complement-driven cytotoxic mechanism that does not involve NK cells or CD16.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opsonization and phagocytosis is a separate type 2 route in which Fc receptors on phagocytes engulf antibody-coated cells, not NK-mediated killing.

questions.stem: During sensitization in a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction, a B cell that has captured allergen is induced to class-switch and produce IgE. Which of the following pairs of signals from a Th2 cell drives this class switch?

explanation.summary: Th2-derived IL-4 and CD40L drive B cells to class-switch to IgE during type 1 sensitization.
explanation.whyCorrect: After a B cell internalizes allergen and presents it on MHC II to a Th2 cell, the Th2 cell provides IL-4 and CD40L. These signals drive the B cell to class-switch to IgE and differentiate into IgE-producing plasma cells or memory B cells, priming the individual for a type 1 reaction on re-exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3b and C5a are complement fragments involved in opsonization and neutrophil recruitment, not IgE class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine and heparin are preformed mast cell mediators released during degranulation, not signals that drive B-cell class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IFN-gamma and IL-12 promote Th1 responses and macrophage activation, not IgE class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin and granzyme are cytotoxic effector molecules of CD8+ T and NK cells, not B-cell class-switch signals.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with severe persistent allergic asthma that remains poorly controlled despite inhaled therapy is started on omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody. Which of the following best describes how this drug reduces her allergic responses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds the Fc portion of free IgE, preventing FcεRI binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks the histamine receptor on bronchial smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links FcεRI on mast cells to force receptor internalization

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits the synthesis of leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4

choices.label: E
choices.text: It neutralizes IL-5 so that eosinophils are no longer produced

explanation.summary: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds the Fc portion of circulating IgE so it cannot attach to FcεRI on mast cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The key cause of many allergic disorders is IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells being cross-linked by antigen. Omalizumab, an antibody derived from a single B cell, binds the Fc portion of circulating IgE. Because FcεRI recognizes exactly that Fc region of the IgE heavy chain, the drug prevents IgE from arming mast cells, so allergen exposure can no longer trigger degranulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking histamine receptors would only counter one preformed mediator; omalizumab acts upstream on IgE itself, not on histamine signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cross-linking FcεRI is precisely what triggers degranulation; omalizumab prevents IgE from ever occupying the receptor rather than engaging it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukotriene synthesis is not the target; omalizumab prevents the IgE-FcεRI interaction that precedes any mediator release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 promotes eosinophil production during the late phase, but omalizumab is directed against IgE, not IL-5.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with allergic rhinitis undergoes intradermal allergen skin testing. A wheal-and-flare develops at 15 minutes and fades within an hour. Eight hours later the test site becomes swollen and indurated again, and a biopsy of the site shows infiltration by eosinophils and lymphocytes. Which of the following best explains the reaction at 8 hours?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokines and chemokines newly made by mast cells and basophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial cells lysed by the membrane attack complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complexes deposited in small dermal vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory T cells activated by peptide on MHC class II

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preformed histamine released from mast cell granules

explanation.summary: The late-phase response of a type 1 reaction occurs 6-24 hours after FcεRI cross-linking and is driven by newly synthesized mast cell and basophil mediators.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 1 reactions occur in two phases. The early phase, within seconds, is caused by preformed mediators and produces the wheal-and-flare. From 6 to 24 hours later, mast cells and basophils synthesize new mediators, including TNF-alpha, IL-4, IL-13, IL-3, IL-5, GM-CSF, chemokines, and lipid mediators. This late phase can show as much or more inflammation than the early phase and is characterized by infiltration of eosinophils and lymphocytes, exactly what the biopsy shows.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Membrane attack complex lysis is a complement-mediated cytotoxic (type 2) mechanism and is not part of an allergen skin test response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism (e.g., the Arthus reaction) and does not follow IgE-mediated skin testing in a sensitized allergic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Memory T-cell activation is the type 4 mechanism and takes 24-72 hours; this reaction at 8 hours with eosinophils is the type 1 late phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preformed histamine is released within seconds and produces the early wheal-and-flare, not a recurrent reaction 8 hours later.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman undergoes skin-prick testing for suspected dust-mite allergy. Fifteen minutes after antigen is placed, a raised, pale, swollen bump appears at the site, surrounded by a ring of redness. Which of the following best accounts for the raised, swollen center of the lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis of keratinocytes induced by cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinoid necrosis from neutrophils activated on immune complexes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infiltration of the dermis by eosinophils and lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leakage of plasma fluid and protein from dilated, congested vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proliferation of dermal mast cells in response to IL-3 and IL-5

explanation.summary: The wheal of the wheal-and-flare reaction is edema produced by vasodilation, vascular congestion, and leakage of plasma fluid and protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The early phase of a type 1 reaction is seen locally in the wheal-and-flare of skin allergy tests. A wheal is a raised, swollen area caused by vasodilation, vascular congestion, and edema as histamine increases vascular permeability. The flare is the surrounding redness, which has substantially less edema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T-cell killing of keratinocytes is the type 4 mechanism of contact dermatitis and takes days, not minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophil-driven necrosis on immune complexes describes the type 3 Arthus reaction, which develops over hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophil and lymphocyte infiltration characterizes the late-phase response at 6-24 hours, not the 15-minute wheal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cells do not proliferate within minutes; IL-3 and IL-5 are late-phase cytokines that promote eosinophils.

questions.stem: Compared with histamine, the leukotrienes (C4, D4, and E4) released by activated mast cells are best characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ability to trigger further histamine release from neighboring mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anticoagulant activity that limits clotting at the site of degranulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct chemoattraction of monocytes, lymphocytes, and neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease activity that remodels the surrounding connective tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Roughly 1000-fold greater potency at increasing vascular permeability

explanation.summary: Leukotrienes are very potent bronchoconstrictors that increase vascular permeability about 1000 times more than histamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 are lipid mediators of the type 1 reaction that cause smooth muscle contraction, bronchial constriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion. They are very potent bronchoconstrictors and increase vascular permeability roughly 1000 times more than histamine, which is one reason epinephrine is given to counteract them during anaphylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Triggering histamine release from mast cells is the action of eosinophil-derived major basic protein, not leukotrienes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticoagulant activity is the property of heparin, a preformed toxic mediator, not of leukotrienes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Attracting monocytes, eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils is the role of chemokines made in the late phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Connective tissue remodeling is the role of tryptase and other mast cell proteases, not lipid mediators.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man develops wheezing, hypotension, and lip swelling minutes after a wasp sting and is given intramuscular epinephrine. Which of the following effects of epinephrine best explains why it is given in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds free IgE and prevents its attachment to FcεRI

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks class-switching of B cells to IgE production

choices.label: C
choices.text: It degrades histamine that has already been released into tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents cross-linking of FcεRI on sensitized mast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, counteracting leukotrienes and PAF

explanation.summary: Epinephrine is given after an allergic reaction because it induces bronchial relaxation, counteracting the bronchoconstriction caused by leukotrienes and PAF.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipid mediators released by mast cells, including leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor, cause smooth muscle contraction and bronchial constriction, producing the wheezing and bronchospasm of anaphylaxis. One of the reasons epinephrine is given is that it induces bronchial relaxation, directly opposing these mediators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding the Fc portion of free IgE is the mechanism of omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody used for prevention, not of epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Class-switching to IgE is driven by IL-4 and CD40L during sensitization; epinephrine has no role in this step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine does not degrade histamine; it acts on smooth muscle to reverse the effects of released mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine does not act on FcεRI; by the time it is given, cross-linking and degranulation have already occurred.

questions.stem: Within seconds of FcεRI cross-linking, mast cells release mediators stored in their granules, whereas other mediators appear only 6 to 24 hours later because they must first be synthesized. Which of the following mediators belongs to the first, preformed group?

explanation.summary: Heparin is a preformed toxic mediator released within seconds of mast cell degranulation, whereas cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-5, IL-13, and GM-CSF are newly made in the late phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within seconds of FcεRI cross-linking, mast cells release preformed inflammatory mediators that begin the early phase. These include the toxic mediators histamine (a vasoactive amine) and heparin (an anticoagulant), lipid mediators, and enzymes such as tryptase. Heparin is therefore a preformed granule mediator.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GM-CSF is a late-phase cytokine promoting eosinophils; it is not stored preformed in mast cell granules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-13 is a late-phase cytokine that, with IL-4, perpetuates the Th2 immune response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-5 is a late-phase cytokine that, with IL-3 and GM-CSF, promotes eosinophil production and activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is a late-phase cytokine synthesized 6-24 hours after cross-linking that promotes inflammation.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with poorly controlled asthma has a sputum sample showing abundant eosinophils. During the late phase of his type 1 reactions, which of the following groups of mast cell-derived cytokines is most responsible for promoting the production and activation of these eosinophils?

explanation.summary: IL-3, IL-5, and GM-CSF made by mast cells in the late phase promote the production and activation of eosinophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: From 6 to 24 hours after FcεRI cross-linking, mast cells and basophils synthesize new cytokines. Among these, IL-3, IL-5, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) promote the production and activation of eosinophils, whose infiltration is a hallmark of the late-phase reaction and of allergic diseases such as asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma and IL-12 are associated with Th1 responses and macrophage activation in type 4 reactions, not eosinophilic type 1 inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-2 and IL-4 are secreted by dendritic cells during sensitization to polarize naive T cells toward Th2, not to generate eosinophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 and IL-13 perpetuate the Th2 immune response; they are not the eosinophil-promoting cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha promotes inflammation and chemokines attract cells, but neither drives eosinophil production the way IL-3, IL-5, and GM-CSF do.

questions.stem: A biopsy of nasal mucosa from a patient with chronic allergic rhinitis shows dense eosinophilic infiltration. Eosinophils in this tissue release a toxic protein that triggers histamine release from nearby mast cells and normally functions in defense against parasites. Which of the following is this protein?

explanation.summary: Activated eosinophils release major basic protein, a toxic protein that functions in parasite defense but also amplifies the allergic response by triggering mast cell histamine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eosinophilic inflammation is a hallmark of many allergic diseases and amplifies the immune response. Activated eosinophils release cytokines, chemokines, and lipid mediators like mast cells do, and in addition make toxic proteins such as major basic protein (MBP). MBP triggers histamine release from mast cells, amplifying the allergic response, and normally functions in parasite defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heparin is a preformed mast cell anticoagulant, not an eosinophil product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukotriene C4 is a lipid mediator that causes bronchoconstriction and vascular permeability; it is not a protein and does not act by triggering histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet-activating factor is a lipid mediator causing smooth muscle contraction and vascular permeability, not a toxic protein that triggers histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tryptase is a mast cell enzyme that remodels connective tissue and serves as a marker of mast cell degranulation; it is not an eosinophil toxic protein.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the receptor through which IgE sensitizes mast cells in a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complement receptor (CR1) that binds C3b-coated immune complexes on erythrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-affinity receptor for the Fc of the IgE heavy chain on mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-affinity receptor for the Fab region of IgE that is expressed only on plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor for the Fc of IgG (CD16) that triggers release of perforin and granzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor for the IgE light chain that is expressed on Th2 helper cells

explanation.summary: FcεRI is a high-affinity receptor for the Fc portion of the IgE heavy chain, found on mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: In step 3 of sensitization, circulating IgE is bound by FcεRI on mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. FcεRI has a high affinity for the Fc portion of the IgE heavy chain. When enough IgE is bound to a cell that the addition of antigen will cause degranulation, the cell is said to be sensitized.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CR1 on erythrocytes shuttles C3b-coated immune complexes to splenic phagocytes; it does not bind IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcεRI is high-affinity and binds the Fc, not the Fab, portion of IgE; plasma cells secrete IgE rather than binding it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD16 (FcγRIII) is the IgG receptor on NK cells that mediates ADCC in type 2 reactions, not the IgE receptor of type 1 reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FcεRI binds the heavy chain Fc region, not the light chain, and it is expressed on mast cells rather than on Th2 cells.

questions.stem: During sensitization to an inhaled allergen, dendritic cells that have taken up the allergen migrate to a draining lymph node and present peptide-MHC II complexes to naive T cells. Which of the following cytokines secreted by these dendritic cells drives the naive T cells toward the Th2 phenotype?

explanation.summary: Activated dendritic cells in secondary lymphoid organs present peptide-MHC II to naive T cells and secrete IL-2 and IL-4, driving Th2 differentiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In step 2 of type 1 sensitization (IgE production), activated dendritic cells migrate to secondary lymphoid organs, where they present peptide-MHC II complexes to naive T cells and secrete IL-2 and IL-4. Naive T cells activated in this context differentiate into Th2 cells, which subsequently help allergen-specific B cells class-switch to IgE.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-12 and IFN-gamma promote Th1 responses and macrophage activation, as in the type 4 PPD reaction, not Th2 polarization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-3 and IL-5 are late-phase mast cell cytokines that promote eosinophil production, not dendritic cell signals to naive T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 and CD40L are the signals a Th2 cell provides to a B cell to drive IgE class-switching; CD40L is a surface ligand, not a dendritic cell-secreted cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha and IL-13 are late-phase mediators made by mast cells after degranulation; they are not the dendritic cell cytokines that polarize naive T cells.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy eats a peanut butter sandwich for the first time without any reaction. Two months later, a few minutes after eating peanuts again, he develops hives and lip swelling. Which of the following best explains why the first exposure caused no symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allergen-specific IgE had not yet been produced and bound to mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement regulators such as CD55 blocked the initial reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mast cells had not yet migrated into the mucosa on the first exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regulatory T cells suppressed the response until the second exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first dose contained too little allergen to activate mast cells

explanation.summary: Virtually all hypersensitivity reactions first require sensitization, an initial exposure that generates a memory response priming the immune system for a greater response.
explanation.whyCorrect: A type 1 reaction requires that the individual already be sensitized: on first exposure, dendritic cells present the allergen, Th2 cells are generated, B cells class-switch to IgE, and IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells. Only after enough allergen-specific IgE is bound to mast cells will re-exposure cross-link FcεRI and cause degranulation. The first exposure builds this memory response without producing symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD55 and CD59 limit membrane attack complex formation in type 2 reactions and play no role in IgE-mediated allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells are already resident in tissues; what is missing on first exposure is allergen-specific IgE bound to their FcεRI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick's model of sensitization involves generation of a memory IgE response, not transient suppression by regulatory T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The amount of allergen is not the issue; without preexisting allergen-specific IgE on mast cells, no dose can trigger degranulation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and hematuria. Studies show antibodies bound directly to an extracellular matrix protein in the basement membranes of his glomeruli and alveoli, with complement and activated phagocytes at these sites but little direct lysis of the underlying cells. He is diagnosed with Goodpasture's syndrome. Which of the following best classifies the mechanism of his tissue injury?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2 hypersensitivity, inflammation without cell death

explanation.summary: Goodpasture's syndrome is an inflammatory type 2 hypersensitivity in which antibody bound to an extracellular matrix protein triggers inflammation without cell death.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some type 2 reactions, antibody binding to a cell-surface or extracellular matrix protein stimulates an immune response without killing the cell. Complement activation or phagocyte activation via C5a, C3a, or Fc receptors produces inflammation, with activated phagocytes releasing granule contents including reactive oxygen species. Because the antigen is tissue-bound, pathology is organ-specific. Acute rheumatic fever and Goodpasture's syndrome are the brick's examples of this inflammatory type 2 mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The late phase of a type 1 reaction is IgE-driven with eosinophil infiltration; it does not involve antibody bound to basement membrane matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cellular dysregulation describes antibodies that inhibit or amplify cell function, as in myasthenia gravis and Graves disease, not inflammatory damage to basement membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 reactions involve antibody binding soluble antigen to form circulating immune complexes; here the antibody binds a fixed extracellular matrix protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD8+ T-cell cytolysis is a type 4 mechanism, but the injury here is antibody-mediated, not T-cell-mediated.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman receiving high-dose intravenous penicillin for 10 days develops fatigue and pallor. Laboratory studies show a falling hemoglobin and a positive direct antiglobulin test with IgG on her erythrocytes; the anemia resolves after the drug is stopped. Which of the following best classifies this adverse drug reaction?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type 2, antibody-mediated blockade of a cell-surface receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2, antibody-mediated opsonization and destruction of erythrocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 3, immune complexes of drug and antibody depositing in vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 4, drug acting as a hapten to prime cytotoxic T cells

explanation.summary: Penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia is a cytotoxic type 2 hypersensitivity in which antibody-coated erythrocytes are destroyed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse drug reactions such as penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia are listed among the disorders arising from the cytotoxic type 2 response, alongside autoimmune hemolytic anemia, transfusion reactions, and Rh incompatibility. IgG and IgM are opsonins: antibody recognizing antigen on the erythrocyte surface is recognized by Fc receptors on phagocytes, and complement deposition adds C3b, leading to cell death by phagocytosis, complement activation, or ADCC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE-mediated degranulation causes hives, wheezing, or anaphylaxis within minutes, not a gradual antibody-coated hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor blockade is the cellular dysregulation form of type 2 seen in myasthenia gravis; it alters function without cell death, whereas this patient's red cells are being destroyed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 reactions involve soluble antigen and immune complexes that cause vasculitis, nephritis, and arthritis, not IgG fixed on erythrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A hapten priming T cells describes type 4 contact dermatitis; the erythrocyte destruction here is antibody-mediated, not T-cell-mediated.

questions.stem: A splenic macrophage engulfs an erythrocyte that is coated with IgG and with the complement fragment C3b. Which of the following pairs of macrophage receptors mediates recognition of this opsonized cell?

explanation.summary: Phagocytes recognize opsonized cells through Fc receptors that bind antibody and C3b receptors that bind deposited complement.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgG and IgM are opsonins, or phagocytosis enhancers. Antibodies bound to cell-surface antigen are recognized by Fc receptors on phagocytes, inducing phagocytosis. Complement activation also deposits C3b, another opsonin, which is recognized by the phagocyte's C3b receptor. Together these two receptors allow the macrophage to internalize and destroy the opsonized cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD16 is the IgG receptor on NK cells that drives ADCC, and the T-cell receptor recognizes peptide-MHC; neither is the macrophage's phagocytic receptor pair.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CR1 on erythrocytes shuttles immune complexes to the spleen, and CD59 is a regulatory protein that blocks MAC formation; neither mediates macrophage uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FcεRI binds IgE on mast cells and the C5a receptor mediates chemotaxis; they do not recognize IgG- and C3b-coated cells for phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class II and CD40 are involved in antigen presentation and T-cell help, not in recognizing opsonins on a target cell.

questions.stem: Immunofluorescence on a tissue biopsy from a patient with an immune-mediated disease shows that the pathogenic antibody is IgM. Based on the classification of hypersensitivity reactions by immune reactant, which of the following could this reaction represent?

explanation.summary: Type 1 reactions are driven by IgE, types 2 and 3 involve IgM and IgG, and type 4 reactions are mediated by T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The four categories of hypersensitivity are distinguished by mechanism of pathology. Type 1 reactions are driven by IgE; types 2 and 3 involve IgM and IgG antibodies (against cell- or matrix-bound antigen in type 2 and soluble antigen in type 3); and type 4 reactions are mediated by T cells. An IgM-mediated reaction is therefore type 2 or type 3.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 reactions are mediated by IgE bound to FcεRI, not by IgM.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 2 can involve IgM, but type 1 is IgE-driven, so this pairing is wrong.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 can involve IgM, but type 4 reactions are T-cell-mediated and involve no pathogenic antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 4 reactions are mediated by CD4+ or CD8+ T cells, not by antibody of any class.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has a sore throat caused by group A streptococcus that goes untreated. Her parents ask about her risk of developing acute rheumatic fever. Approximately what proportion of individuals with untreated group A streptococcal infection develop this complication?

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever occurs in 1-3% of individuals with an untreated group A streptococcal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute rheumatic fever is an inflammatory type 2 hypersensitivity that develops in 1-3% of people with untreated group A streptococcus infection. It is characterized by arthritis, rash, and cardiac inflammation appearing a few weeks after resolution of the infection, as a result of molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and a cardiac protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fewer than 0.1% understates the risk; the brick gives a figure of 1-3%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 10-15% overstates the risk; only a small minority, 1-3%, of untreated infections lead to rheumatic fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25-30% is far higher than the 1-3% cited; rheumatic fever is an uncommon complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About half of untreated patients do not develop rheumatic fever; the risk is 1-3%.

questions.stem: A researcher studies why immune complexes formed during ordinary infections rarely cause disease in healthy people. Which of the following best describes the normal mechanism that clears these complexes from the circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD55 and CD59 on endothelial cells dissociate antigen from antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocytes bind the complexes via CR1 and shuttle them to splenic phagocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mast cells bind the complexes via FcεRI and degrade them after degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils attracted by C5a destroy the complexes within the vessel wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: NK cells bind the complexes via CD16 and release perforin and granzymes

explanation.summary: Immune complexes formed during normal antigen exposure are cleared when erythrocytes carry them to splenic phagocytes via CR1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immune system forms immune complexes during normal antigen exposure, but these are cleared when erythrocytes shuttle them to splenic phagocytes via CR1. Type 3 disease arises only when plasma cells produce antibody at an accelerated rate and vast amounts of antigen are present, so that more complexes form than this pathway can clear, allowing deposition in tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD55 and CD59 are regulatory proteins that block membrane attack complex formation on cells such as erythrocytes; they do not dissociate immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcεRI binds IgE, not IgG-containing immune complexes, and mast cell degranulation causes allergic symptoms rather than clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil recruitment by C5a to deposited complexes is the mechanism of type 3 tissue damage, not of harmless clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD16 on NK cells recognizes IgG bound to cell-surface antigen for ADCC in type 2 reactions; it is not the clearance route for circulating complexes.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a type 3 hypersensitivity disorder has proteinuria, a purpuric rash on her legs, and painful swollen joints, although the antigen driving her immune complexes originated in a distant tissue. Which of the following best explains the distribution of her lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies in the complexes cross-react with kidney, skin, and joint antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating complexes deposit in small, high-pressure vessels of these tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complexes form locally in each affected organ where antigen is produced

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mast cells in these tissues carry IgE directed against the complexed antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Memory T cells home specifically to the glomeruli, dermis, and synovium

explanation.summary: Immune complexes circulate and deposit preferentially in small vessels under high pressure, such as those of the glomeruli, skin, and joints, so the site of damage need not match the site of formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immune complexes are likely to deposit in blood vessels, especially small vessels at high pressure such as those in the glomeruli, skin, and joints. Type 3 reactions are therefore characterized by nephritis, arthritis, systemic vasculitis, and cutaneous vasculitis. Because complexes circulate, the site of damage does not necessarily reflect the original site of formation, which is why disease can be systemic even when the antigen came from one location.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cross-reactivity of antibody with tissue antigens describes molecular mimicry in type 2 acute rheumatic fever, not immune complex deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type 3 complexes form in the circulation and are carried to deposition sites; the site of damage does not necessarily reflect the site of formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE on mast cells mediates type 1 reactions and does not determine where immune complexes deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 damage is antibody- and neutrophil-mediated after complex deposition; T-cell homing is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who has received several prior doses of a vaccine is given another intradermal booster. Six hours later the injection site is markedly swollen and edematous, and a biopsy shows neutrophils, complement bound within small vessels, and fibroid necrosis. Which of the following best describes the underlying process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of memory Th1 cells and macrophages by the antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linking of IgE on dermal mast cells by the vaccine antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Destruction of antibody-coated cells by NK cells through ADCC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Local deposition of immune complexes formed with preexisting IgG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic serum sickness triggered by foreign protein in the vaccine

explanation.summary: The Arthus reaction is a localized type 3 hypersensitivity in which repeat intradermal antigen meets preexisting systemic IgG, causing local immune complex deposition within hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the classic Arthus reaction, intradermal immunization generates systemic IgG toward the vaccination antigen. On subsequent intradermal immunization, immune complexes form and deposit at the site of the second injection. Complement binds the complexes, C5a and C3a attract neutrophils, and the result is a local, subacute inflammatory reaction with inflammation, edema, and potentially fibroid necrosis, occurring within hours because the antibody already exists.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Memory Th1 and macrophage activation is the type 4 mechanism of the PPD test, which takes 24-72 hours and produces induration, not vascular necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE cross-linking would produce a wheal-and-flare within minutes, not neutrophils, complement deposition, and necrosis at 6 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADCC is a type 2 mechanism directed at antibody-coated cells; the lesion here is caused by immune complexes in vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum sickness is a systemic type 3 reaction with fever, rash, and arthralgias; the Arthus reaction is the localized counterpart confined to the injection site.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old rancher was treated with horse-derived antivenom after a rattlesnake bite 3 years ago and developed fever, rash, and arthralgias 10 days later. He is bitten again and receives the same antivenom. This time, fever, rash, and joint pain begin within hours of the infusion. Which of the following best explains the shorter interval on this occasion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher dose of antivenom was administered on this occasion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies from a memory response formed immune complexes at once

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE made after the first exposure cross-linked FcεRI on mast cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory T cells primed by the first exposure were rapidly reactivated

choices.label: E
choices.text: The venom itself acted as a superantigen and activated many T cells

explanation.summary: Type 3 damage from a new foreign antigen takes 1-2 weeks, but on re-exposure a memory response provides preformed antibody so pathology occurs within hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: The primary response to a new foreign antigen takes time, requiring T-cell activation, B-cell activation, and class-switching, so serum sickness after a first exposure appears 1-2 weeks later. If exposure has occurred more than once and the response is a memory response, antibody is already present, immune complexes form immediately, and pathology can occur within hours. Type 3 reactions typically occur within 6 hours of exposure but can take as long as 10 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dose does not change the kinetics of antibody production; the interval shortened because antibody already existed before the second infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE cross-linking causes anaphylaxis within minutes with hives and bronchospasm, not a delayed-by-hours syndrome of fever, rash, and joint pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Memory T-cell reactivation is the type 4 mechanism and takes 24-72 hours; serum sickness is an antibody-mediated type 3 reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigens are bacterial toxins that bind TCR and MHC II; fever, rash, and arthralgias after antivenom are immune complex-mediated, not superantigen-driven.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has had years of gradually worsening, symmetric swelling and stiffness of the small joints of her hands. Serum testing detects rheumatoid factor. Which of the following best describes this autoantibody?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE directed against a synovial allergen

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG directed against a soluble microbial protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgG that blocks a receptor on synovial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgM directed against a cell-surface blood group antigen

explanation.summary: Rheumatoid factor is an autoimmune IgM antibody directed toward self-IgG and contributes to the immune complex pathology of rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatoid arthritis is a type 3 immune complex disease. In RA, an autoimmune IgM antibody called rheumatoid factor, directed toward self-IgG, is part of the pathophysiology. In autoimmune type 3 disease the antigen is always present but typically at low levels, so pathology is insidious and prolonged, matching this patient's years of slowly progressive joint disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE against an allergen mediates type 1 reactions with immediate symptoms, not chronic immune complex arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody against a soluble microbial protein describes serum sickness or similar foreign-antigen type 3 reactions, not the self-directed rheumatoid factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A receptor-blocking IgG describes the cellular dysregulation form of type 2 (e.g., myasthenia gravis), not rheumatoid factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgM against a blood group antigen describes cytotoxic type 2 reactions such as transfusion reactions, not the anti-IgG antibody of rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman develops high fever, hypotension, and a diffuse rash within a day of a staphylococcal infection of a surgical wound. Laboratory studies show extremely high levels of circulating cytokines, and a large fraction of her T cells are activated. Which of the following best explains the massive T-cell activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacterial toxin bridged the TCR and MHC II, activating T cells independent of antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial peptides were presented on MHC II to many antigen-specific T-cell clones

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hapten-modified skin proteins primed a large pool of memory T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE against staphylococcal antigens cross-linked FcεRI on tissue mast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complexes of toxin and IgG activated complement throughout the body

explanation.summary: Superantigens are bacterial toxins that bind the TCR and MHC II directly, activating up to 70% of T cells in an antigen-independent manner with massive cytokine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The superantigen response is one of the common examples of type 4 hypersensitivity. Superantigens are bacterial toxins that bind to the TCR and MHC II, inducing the same signaling as a cognate TCR-MHC-peptide interaction. Because this bypasses antigen specificity, the result is pan-activation of T cells, up to 70% of them, with release of high levels of cytokines that produce fever, hypotension, and rash.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Conventional peptide presentation activates only the rare clones specific for that peptide, not a large fraction of all T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haptens such as pentadecylcatechol prime antigen-specific T cells for contact dermatitis over 10-15 days, not massive nonspecific activation within a day.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is a type 1 mechanism producing hives and bronchospasm, not widespread T-cell activation with cytokine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complex deposition is a type 3 mechanism causing vasculitis and nephritis; it does not activate T cells en masse.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student clears brush for the first time and, 12 days later, develops an itchy vesicular rash where poison ivy touched his arms. The following summer, a similar rash appears only 2 days after exposure. Which of the following best explains the difference in timing between the two episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Class-switching of B cells to IgG took longer during the first episode

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune complexes needed more time to accumulate on the first exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: More pentadecylcatechol penetrated intact skin on the second exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Naive T-cell priming takes 10-15 days, whereas memory T cells respond in 24-72 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first rash was a type 1 reaction, whereas the second was a type 4 reaction

explanation.summary: Type 4 sensitization requires priming of CD4+ or CD8+ T cells over 10-15 days or more, but primed T cells induce pathology within 24-72 hours of secondary exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because T cells mediate the damage in type 4 reactions, sensitization requires antigen presentation by APCs and priming of CD4+ or CD8+ T cells, a phase that can take 10 to 15 days or more. With secondary exposure, primed memory T cells can induce pathology in 24-72 hours. Pentadecylcatechol bound to skin proteins primes T cells and generates memory on first exposure; on later exposures those memory T cells cause contact dermatitis quickly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Contact dermatitis is T-cell-mediated; antibody class-switching is not the rate-limiting step in either episode.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune complex accumulation is the mechanism of type 3 reactions, not of hapten-driven contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The amount of hapten penetrating the skin does not explain a 12-day versus 2-day difference; the presence of primed memory T cells does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both episodes are type 4 contact dermatitis; a type 1 reaction would occur within minutes, not 12 days.

questions.stem: A biopsy of a vesicular skin lesion from a patient with contact dermatitis shows apoptotic epidermal cells adjacent to infiltrating lymphocytes. Which of the following best describes the cell and mechanism directly killing the epidermal cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4+ helper T cells secreting IFN-gamma that activates macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ T cells recognizing antigen on MHC I and releasing perforin and granzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosinophils releasing major basic protein onto epidermal cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils recruited by C5a releasing reactive oxygen species

choices.label: E
choices.text: NK cells recognizing IgG-coated cells through CD16 (FcγRIII)

explanation.summary: In type 4 cytotoxicity, CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize antigen on MHC I and release perforin and granzymes, inducing apoptosis of skin cells and producing vesicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (CTLs) recognize foreign antigens presented in MHC I and become activated. The activated CD8+ T cell releases perforin and granzymes, which perforate the cell membrane and induce apoptosis. Cytotoxicity of skin cells from CTL activation produces the vesicles of contact dermatitis, some of which rupture to leave red, inflamed open sores. The brick summarizes contact dermatitis as cytotoxicity from cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4+ helper T cells secreting IFN-gamma to activate macrophages is the type 4 mechanism of the PPD skin test, producing induration rather than direct epidermal cell apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophil major basic protein amplifies type 1 allergic responses by triggering mast cell histamine release; it is not the effector of contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil recruitment by C5a with reactive oxygen species is a type 2 or type 3 inflammatory mechanism, not the cytotoxic T-cell response of contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK-cell ADCC via CD16 is a type 2 antibody-dependent mechanism, and contact dermatitis is T-cell-mediated without antibody coating of skin cells.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops sneezing, watery eyes, and hives every spring when tree pollen counts rise. Her physician explains that the underlying process is a type 1 (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction. Production of which of the following antibodies is required for this pathophysiology?

explanation.summary: Classic allergy is a type 1 (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states allergic reactions are mediated by IgE, which recognizes allergens and binds mast cells through the high-affinity FcepsilonRI receptor. Cross-linking of IgE by allergen triggers degranulation and the release of allergic mediators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is involved in mucosal humoral immunity and is one of the milder 'blocking' antibodies favored by desensitization, not the driver of type 1 hypersensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD sits on the membrane of mature B cells and does not mediate the allergic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG is a blocking antibody that immunotherapy shifts the response toward; it is not the cause of the allergic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM participates in the humoral response to antigen but does not mediate type 1 hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with a shellfish allergy after developing severe lip swelling, throat tightness, and respiratory distress 15 minutes after eating shrimp. He asks how he can best prevent another reaction like this. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

explanation.summary: Allergen avoidance is the most effective way to prevent allergic reactions, especially after a severe or anaphylactic event.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states avoidance is the first step in managing allergies and is crucial in individuals with a previous anaphylactic reaction. Orally ingested allergens such as shellfish are among the most easily avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Epinephrine treats an active anaphylactic reaction and does not prevent one; it is a rescue medication, not prevention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunotherapy has a role for some allergies (for example, insect venom) but is not the recommended approach for severe shellfish allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihistamines treat histamine-mediated symptoms but do not prevent a severe reaction from occurring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corticosteroids control inflammation as treatment; they are not a preventive strategy.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is stung by a hornet and within minutes develops diffuse hives, throat tightness, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

explanation.summary: Intramuscular epinephrine is the first and most important treatment for anaphylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that an intramuscular injection of epinephrine is the most critical, first medication in anaphylaxis. It causes bronchodilation to relieve respiratory distress and, through alpha receptors, vasoconstriction that reverses hypotension and edema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inhaled beta-2 agonist helps bronchospasm but does not address the hypotension or systemic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids reduce the late-phase reaction but are not the first-line, life-saving agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravenous fluids support blood pressure as an adjunct in severe cases, but epinephrine is the primary and first treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antihistamines are part of the treatment cocktail but are adjunctive and do not reverse airway or cardiovascular collapse.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in anaphylactic shock is given intramuscular epinephrine, and his low blood pressure improves. Which of the following actions of epinephrine is most directly responsible for raising his blood pressure?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of the CysLT1 leukotriene receptor

explanation.summary: Epinephrine raises blood pressure in anaphylaxis chiefly through alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states epinephrine activates alpha-1 receptors to reduce edema and vascular permeability and to cause vasoconstriction of blood vessels, thereby supporting blood pressure and circulation in the patient with anaphylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-2 bronchodilation opens the airways to relieve respiratory distress but does not directly raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 receptor blockade is the mechanism of antihistamines, not epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking the CysLT1 receptor is the mechanism of antileukotrienes and is unrelated to epinephrine's pressor effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppression of cytokine transcription is the mechanism of corticosteroids, not epinephrine.

questions.stem: During an allergic reaction, mast cells release mediators in two phases. Which of the following mediators is pre-formed and released immediately during the early-phase response?

explanation.summary: Histamine, along with heparin and tryptase, is a pre-formed mediator released immediately in the early-phase mast cell response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the early-phase response as the immediate release of pre-formed molecules, including toxic metabolites (histamine and heparin) and enzymes (tryptase).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-5 is a newly synthesized cytokine of the late phase that recruits eosinophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukotriene C4 is a newly synthesized lipid mediator released in the late phase, delayed by the time needed for synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet-activating factor is a lipid mediator newly synthesized in the late phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is a newly synthesized cytokine released in the late phase.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with hypotension and stridor shortly after a bee sting, but the clinical picture is confusing and other causes are being considered. Which of the following laboratory findings would best support a diagnosis of anaphylaxis?

explanation.summary: Serum tryptase, released by mast cells, rises within minutes of anaphylaxis and helps confirm the diagnosis when it is uncertain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states tryptase, produced primarily by mast cells, can be elevated within minutes and persist for several hours after anaphylaxis begins, making it useful for diagnosing anaphylaxis when there is uncertainty.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allergy involves IgE sensitization; a decrease in IgE is not a marker of an acute anaphylactic episode.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C-reactive protein is a nonspecific inflammatory marker and is not specific for mast cell activation or anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgA is a blocking antibody and is not a diagnostic marker for acute anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A skin prick test identifies specific allergens but is not used to diagnose an acute anaphylactic reaction.

questions.stem: A physician wants to identify the specific allergens triggering a patient's seasonal allergic rhinitis. Which of the following is the most common and most sensitive method used to identify specific allergens?

explanation.summary: The skin prick (puncture) test is the most common and most sensitive method to identify specific allergens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states skin prick/puncture testing is the most common and most sensitive method; it introduces a small amount of allergen into the skin and looks for a wheal-and-flare reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood testing with ELISA measures allergen-specific IgE but is less sensitive than skin testing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Challenge testing is riskier and is not the primary choice for identifying triggering allergens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A complete blood count is a general blood count and is not an allergen-identification test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Flow cytometry identifies specific cell lineages, not which allergens cause a reaction.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has atopic dermatitis and allergic rhinitis, and both his mother and sister have asthma. His pediatrician explains he has a genetic predisposition to develop IgE sensitization to allergens. Which of the following terms best describes this predisposition?

explanation.summary: Atopy is the genetic predisposition to develop IgE sensitization, associated with a personal or family history of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines atopy as a genetic predisposition to develop IgE sensitization to allergens, usually implying a personal or family history of atopic conditions such as atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An anaphylactoid reaction is an anaphylaxis-like reaction driven by non-IgE mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction, not an inherited predisposition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Desensitization is a form of immunotherapy (a treatment), not a predisposition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sensitization describes a mast cell already loaded with allergen-specific IgE, not the inherited predisposition itself.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe allergic asthma remains symptomatic despite inhaled corticosteroids and is started on omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody. Which of the following best describes its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds free IgE and prevents it from attaching to FcepsilonRI

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks H1 histamine receptors on mast cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocks the cysteinyl leukotriene CysLT1 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle

explanation.summary: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds free IgE, preventing it from attaching to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states omalizumab binds to IgE and prevents it from attaching to FcepsilonRI receptors on mast cells and basophils, thereby reducing allergic mediator release; it is used in moderate-to-severe allergic asthma and chronic spontaneous urticaria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H1 receptor blockade is the mechanism of antihistamines, not omalizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking the CysLT1 receptor is the mechanism of antileukotrienes such as montelukast and zafirlukast.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stimulating beta-2 receptors is the mechanism of beta-agonists such as albuterol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppressing cytokine transcription is the mechanism of corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic asthma undergoes a bronchial biopsy that shows abundant eosinophils in the airway tissue, associated with ongoing inflammation and airway remodeling. Which of the following cytokines is chiefly responsible for recruiting and activating these cells?

explanation.summary: Eosinophils are recruited and activated by IL-5 and drive late-phase tissue damage and airway remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states eosinophils are recruited and activated by IL-5 and play a major role in releasing cytotoxic substances during the late phase, contributing to tissue damage; they are prominent in the tissues of patients with chronic asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3a is a complement anaphylatoxin, not the cytokine that recruits eosinophils here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE is an antibody that sensitizes mast cells; it is not a cytokine that recruits eosinophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma is a Th1 cytokine, not the driver of eosinophilic allergic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukin-2 is chiefly a T-cell growth factor and is not the eosinophil recruiter described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man receives intravenous radiocontrast for a CT scan and, despite no prior exposure, immediately develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension. Testing suggests the reaction is not mediated by IgE. Which of the following terms best describes this reaction?

explanation.summary: An anaphylaxis-like reaction that is not driven by IgE is called an anaphylactoid reaction, classically from opioids and radiocontrast media.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states an anaphylaxis-type reaction, sometimes called 'anaphylactoid,' can be mediated by non-IgE mechanisms and is classically directed at opioids and radiocontrast media.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Atopy is a genetic predisposition to IgE sensitization, not an acute reaction to contrast.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem specifies the reaction is not IgE-mediated and occurred without prior sensitizing exposure, so it is not classic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum sickness is not the mechanism the brick assigns to non-IgE contrast reactions; the brick attributes these to anaphylactoid reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed, T-cell-mediated reaction, not the immediate reaction described here.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old beekeeper has had two episodes of documented IgE-dependent anaphylaxis from bee stings and is referred for subcutaneous immunotherapy (desensitization). Which of the following best describes how this treatment reduces his risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Permanently depletes all mast cells and basophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Provides long-term blockade of H1 histamine receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shifts the immune response away from IgE toward IgG or IgA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suppresses eosinophil production in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Desensitization gives increasing allergen doses to shift the response away from severe IgE toward milder IgG or IgA antibodies that block antigen from activating sensitized cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states desensitization shifts the immune response away from severe IgE responses and toward milder IgG or IgA responses that bind antigen and prevent it from activating sensitized cells; immunotherapy is the preferred treatment for proven IgE-dependent insect venom anaphylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunotherapy does not deplete all mast cells and basophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Long-term H1 receptor blockade describes antihistamines, not desensitization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It does not work by suppressing bone-marrow eosinophil production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Desensitization is active immunotherapy that reshapes the patient's own response; it is not passive antibody transfer.

questions.stem: A public health researcher is reviewing prevalence estimates for allergic conditions in the United States. Which of the following allergic conditions has the highest estimated prevalence?

explanation.summary: Allergic rhinitis is the most prevalent allergic condition, affecting an estimated 10-30% of people.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick cites American Academy of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology estimates: allergic rhinitis 10-30%, drug allergies up to 10%, food allergies 8% of children and 6% of adults, and anaphylaxis in up to 2% of people annually. Allergic rhinitis is the highest of these.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Up to 2% of people experience anaphylaxis annually, the lowest figure listed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drug allergies are estimated at up to 10%, lower than the 10-30% range for allergic rhinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Food allergy affects an estimated 6% of adults.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Food allergy affects an estimated 8% of children, well below the allergic rhinitis estimate.

questions.stem: An emergency department quality committee is analyzing the causes of anaphylaxis cases treated over the past year. Which of the following is the most common trigger of anaphylaxis?

explanation.summary: The most common triggers of anaphylaxis, in order, are medication, food, and insect bites.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common triggers of anaphylaxis are, in this order, medication, food, and insect bites. Up to 2% of people experience anaphylaxis annually, with 500 to 1000 deaths per year in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Animal dander is a common inhaled allergen but is not among the top triggers of anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Food is the second most common trigger of anaphylaxis, behind medications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pollens are common inhaled allergens causing allergic rhinitis but are not listed among the leading triggers of anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insect bites and stings are the third most common trigger, after medications and foods.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops anaphylaxis after receiving an intravenous antibiotic and progresses to overt shock with a blood pressure of 60/30 mm Hg before epinephrine can be administered. His family asks about his prognosis. Once overt shock has developed in anaphylaxis, the mortality rate may approach which of the following?

explanation.summary: Most anaphylaxis resolves with prompt epinephrine, but if overt shock develops the mortality rate may approach 20%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the prognosis for most patients with anaphylaxis is good because most episodes resolve with prompt epinephrine use; however, if overt shock develops, the mortality rate may approach 20%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two percent is the approximate proportion of people who experience anaphylaxis annually, not the mortality of anaphylactic shock.
